node.label: Joan Kelly
node.date_label: The Social Relation of the Sexes (1976) · Did Women Have a Renaissance? (1977) · Women, History, and Theory (1984)
node.description: In “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977), Joan Kelly answered her own question in the negative, arguing that the period saw a relative contraction of the powers of secular women of the courtly and patrician elite. “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976) made relations between women and men part of explanations of historical change and challenged inherited period boundaries. In their 1994 retrospective, Alice Kessler-Harris and Amy Swerdlow quoted Catharine Stimpson’s judgement that Kelly’s investigations “altered the history of the Renaissance and shaped that of women,” and recalled the first M.A. programme in women’s history that Kelly set up with Gerda Lerner. Its claims remained contested: Brian Richardson (2020) wrote that her “partial, blunt and pessimistic assessment” needs to be nuanced considerably in view of what women achieved despite their subordination. Her essays were collected posthumously in Women, History, and Theory (1984; paperback 1986).
node.representative_figures_and_works: “The Social Relation of the Sexes: Methodological Implications of Women’s History” (1976); “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977); “The Doubled Vision of Feminist Theory” (1979); “Early Feminist Theory and the Querelle des Femmes, 1400–1789” (1982); Women, History, and Theory: The Essays of Joan Kelly (1984; paperback 1986).
node.scope_note: The Renaissance essay is represented through Richardson’s preface (2020); the essay itself was not read on a permitted route. The 1976 methodological essay was read in a licensed abridged reprint. Richardson’s preface p. x was read. The complete 1979 and 1982 essays, the collected volume and its introduction, Catharine R. Stimpson’s foreword, and the original works attributed to Kelly’s interlocutors remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976), Kelly draws on Rowbotham’s Woman’s Consciousness, Man’s World (1973) to connect women’s work and family relations with the formation of consciousness.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read licensed abridged reprint in Just Methods, printed pp. 8, 12–13, especially the final substantive paragraph and n. 26, which explicitly attributes its point to Rowbotham’s 1973 book. Notes 6–7 and 23 also name Rowbotham. The argument does not make women a homogeneous economic class. The 1976 journal article is excerpted, and Rowbotham’s original book and Kelly’s separate review of it remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976), Kelly invokes Marx’s account of production as reproducing people and social relations to include procreation and child socialization in the productive work of society.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed abridged primary reprint, Just Methods, printed pp. 10–11, particularly the opening paragraph on p. 11, which expressly attributes the continuous process of reproduction to Marx. This supports Kelly’s stated use of a conception, not endorsement of all Marxist theory or identification of a particular Marx passage. No exact Marx work is supplied in that retained paragraph; original Marx text not collated.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977), Kelly answered her question in the negative, arguing that the period saw a relative contraction of the powers of elite secular women, as Brian Richardson summarises (2020).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read course reprint printed pp. 176–177, which differentiates women’s social positions and cautions about prescriptive sources. Richardson’s preface p. x n. 4 confirms first publication in 1977; the 1994 AHA retrospective describes the intervention’s importance and the Lerner collaboration. Existing women roster row is retained, not duplicated; no person-to-women edge currently exists.
proposed_edges.map_label: Women’s history: no Renaissance for women (1977)

proposed_edges.relationship: “The Social Relation of the Sexes” (1976) treats relations between women and men as historical social relations and makes them part of explanations of social change.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed abridged primary reprint in Just Methods, printed pp. 6–12: introductory formulation; sex as a social category, pp. 8–9; theories of social change, pp. 9–12. The distinction is “social and not a natural one.” Mapping this methodological contribution to the existing gender-history field is editorial, not a claim that Kelly founded that entire field or anticipated every later gender theory. The complete 1976 article remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Polarities, Hybridities: What Strategies for Decentring?’ (2001), Natalie Zemon Davis places Joan Kelly’s ‘Did Women Have a Renaissance?’ (1977) within the social historians’ questioning of the Renaissance as a period, alongside her own decision to restrict the term.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the opening of Davis’s chapter in the licensed University of Toronto Press preview; visually checked printed p. 19. Davis includes herself among social historians who questioned the period’s applicability and explicitly names Kelly’s 1977 intervention. On p. 20 she explains her own more restricted use of Renaissance. The edge records this specific methodological engagement; the passage does not establish Kelly as the sole cause of Davis’s practice. The preview ends during the chapter, so the complete chapter was not read.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Joan Kelly Memorial Prize Marks Its Tenth Year’ (1994), Alice Kessler-Harris and Amy Swerdlow invoke Kelly’s Women, History, and Theory (1984) and describe the prize as a way to continue working in her intellectual spirit.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete AHA article. Its two authors discuss Kelly’s reinterpretation of historical change, recall the intellectual example of her collected essays, and explicitly ask how to continue working in that spirit. This is a jointly stated debt to Kelly’s scholarly example and a specific account of its institutional continuation. It supports no claim that Kessler-Harris adopted a particular Kelly argument. Amy Swerdlow is retained as coauthor in the relationship; she has no permitted endpoint in the supplied lists. No influence on prize recipients is inferred. Reuses packet source jk_w_kessler_swerdlow_1994, freshly checked here.
